source.title: ADAPT: Hybrid Prompt Optimization for LLM Feature Visualization
source.authors: J. Cardoso; Arlindo L. Oliveira; Bruno Martins

record.tranche_reason: Evaluates whether SAE latents in Gemma 2 2B yield interpretable feature visualizations, extending evidence about recoverable features to an LLM setting. It does not test toy-network superposition geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper describes superposition and non-orthogonal directions in its background, citing prior work, but reports no new measurement of feature overlap, sparsity-dependent transitions, capacity competition, or feature dimensionality. Its own result bearing on a claim version is a human evaluation of prompts optimized for SAE latents; optimizer activation comparisons are not direct measurements of representation geometry or SAE feature recovery.
record.test_reason: This is a prompt-optimization methods paper. It uses Gemma Scope SAE latents as a testbed and reports how well its own method (ADAPT) does against GCG, BEAST and EPO, by activation ratio and by human ratings of the optimized prompts. Superposition and non-orthogonal directions appear only as cited background (Elhage et al., 2022). Nothing measures whether features are spread across neurons, whether SAEs recover the model's features, or any toy-model geometry. The human ratings score how readable each optimizer's prompts are, not whether the SAE features exist or are recovered. So no row bears on any version. The reader's T3/V4 'supports' verdict is not warranted.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that ADAPT outperforms GCG, BEAST and EPO in activation (beating GCG on 70.4% of latents) across all layers. They also conclude it yields significantly more interpretable prompts. They argue that high activation correlating with interpretability shows optimization recovers meaningful patterns rather than artifacts. They call LLM feature visualization tractable, given domain-tailored design. They note the evaluation is limited to residual-stream SAEs from one model family.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses SAE-latent prompt optimization and human ratings, not the original toy-network setup or a measurement of superposition geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Human-rated interpretability differs by prompt-generation method: ADAPT scores higher than GCG and GCG with λ = 1.0. The authors report no remarkable interpretability improvement from that fluency penalty. For GCG, higher activation is associated with higher interpretability.

fits_no_version.finding: Prompts optimized to maximally activate Gemma Scope SAE latents in Gemma 2 2B are often rated as showing the latent's pattern (mean ratings 3.78–4.44 on a 1–5 scale). Higher activation correlates with higher interpretability for GCG (r=0.645).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation-maximizing inputs for SAE latents in LLMs recover the latents' human-interpretable patterns. This is about feature-visualization validity, not superposition.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: Evidence for V4 is limited to residual-stream SAEs from one model family and a 60-latent human evaluation. Three raters participated, including an author; explanations were generated by the authors. The paper notes that activation ratio is only a proxy for human interpretability.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded activation-ratio and pairwise optimizer-comparison results in Section 4.2 and Figures 3–5: these compare prompt-optimization methods and do not directly measure SAE feature recovery or representation geometry. Also excluded fluency-weight experiments in Figure 12 because they report optimization activation, not interpretability or recovery.

untested.parts: Toy networks, overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transition and regular geometry are not studied.
Capacity competition, feature importance and dedicated versus shared dimensions are not studied.
Alternative causes of polysemanticity are not studied.
There is no measure of features spread across neurons, and no evaluation of SAE recovery of sparse features. Pre-trained Gemma Scope SAEs are used only as a testbed.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features are not studied.
One-dimensional versus multi-dimensional features are not studied.

record.verdict_notes: The study is a T4 tool-use paper. The reader's 'tests'/T3 classification and the V4 'supports' label are removed. No row measures how features are represented. All rows are method-comparison results for prompt optimizers.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry are not tested.
Capacity pressure, feature importance, dedicated dimensions, and feature sharing are not tested.
The paper does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons or whether polysemanticity is evidence of superposition.
Tests interpretability of prompts optimized for SAE latents in Gemma 2 2B, but not whether features are spread across neurons, other LLMs, or the completeness of SAE recovery.
SAE features' completeness, stability, and canonical status are not tested.
The paper does not compare one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Three raters evaluated prompts generated by GCG for SAE latents.

conditions.value: 60; 50 hardness-weighted plus 10 with activation ratio greater than 1.0

rows.measure: Mean human interpretability rating on a 1–5 scale
rows.note: Ratings assess whether optimized prompts show an interpretable pattern associated with the SAE latent.
rows.check: This is a comparator method's human-rated prompt interpretability (GCG, 3.78). It is a method-comparison value, not a measure of SAE feature recovery or superposition.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Three raters evaluated prompts generated by GCG with a fluency penalty.

conditions.value: 60; 50 hardness-weighted plus 10 with activation ratio greater than 1.0

rows.measure: Mean human interpretability rating on a 1–5 scale
rows.uncertainty: The paper says the penalty did not produce significant changes in human-rated interpretability; no p-value stated for this comparison.
rows.note: The mean rating is above the scale midpoint; authors describe the distribution as remarkably similar to GCG without the penalty.
rows.check: This is a comparator method's rating (GCG with λ=1.0, 3.86) in the study's method comparison. It does not bear on V4.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Three raters evaluated prompts generated by ADAPT for SAE latents.

conditions.value: 60; 50 hardness-weighted plus 10 with activation ratio greater than 1.0

rows.measure: Mean human interpretability rating on a 1–5 scale
rows.uncertainty: Wilcoxon statistic 4459.5, p < 10−8; reported for ADAPT's comparison with the other methods.
rows.note: The authors report ADAPT as significantly better at generating interpretable prompts.
rows.check: This is the study's own method's rating (ADAPT, 4.44) against baselines. The Wilcoxon test is for ADAPT versus the other methods. It is method performance, not evidence on SAE recovery.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured the association between GCG prompt activation ratio and human interpretability ratings.
rows.measure: Pearson correlation between activation ratio and interpretability
rows.note: The paper says higher activation reliably correlates with more interpretable prompts; the reported coefficient is for GCG.
rows.check: This is the correlation between GCG activation ratio and rated interpretability (r=0.645). It validates activation as a proxy for optimizer quality and does not measure feature recovery.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Gemma 2 2B SAE latents; prompts rated for GCG, GCG with λ = 1.0, and ADAPT
reader_labels.reason: Human ratings indicate that optimized prompts often expose understandable or obvious patterns associated with SAE latents, and activation is positively associated with interpretability (r1–r4).
